name: Light Oxblood
lede: Light Oxblood is ColorHub's English rendering of Ebicha, a traditional Japanese color whose kanji name literally means "shrimp brown."

sections.title: Shrimp brown, called maroon
sections.body: The Japanese name is *Ebicha* (海老茶), kanji for "shrimp brown," a dark red-brown our library glosses as "maroon (shrimp brown)" [1]. It is one of the traditional colors of Japan catalogued on Wikipedia; our sources give no date for when the name entered use, and it is undocumented here [1]. The ISCC-NBS system's nearest block is "dark red," 6.5 units away [1]. Nearest on file is [[reddish-wine]] at 2.7 units, with [[chestnut-leather-brown]] close behind at 2.8 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this dark red-brown, as photographed, in 1,097 of 23,781 paintings, 4.61 percent, more common than 82 percent of our named colors; within a single canvas it is a distinct area in 479 of them [2]. Juan de Juanes is its most devoted painter, using it in 4 of 15 works here, 4.4 times the baseline rate of the museums those paintings come from [2]. It peaks in the 1400s, at 5.2 percent of that century's 945 paintings, 2.5 times the expected rate, and inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 49 percent of its 479 appearances [2]. The earliest dated match is from 1260; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first [2]. It shares canvases with [[hay-s-russet]] more often than chance, a lift of 2.8 [2].
